title: "Cassette Response"

As in the movie *RM*, the first speaker left for his mission from Houston. But by the time he returned home from Porto Alegre, his family had moved, and he arrived home to Provo.

Despite his youth, he delivered a measured message that far belied his age—grounded, mature, and remarkably assured.

Following his talk, a newly married returned missionary stood up to sing *"His Eye Is on the Sparrow."* She possessed an angelic voice, reminiscent of a young Charlotte Church.

The congregation was so enchanted by her singing that we hardly noticed the subtle moment when she seamlessly transitioned from English into Spanish.

![](images/20260727_065516~2.jpg)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The final speaker was a woman representing a family that moved into our neighborhood eight years ago.

Many of us still refer to their house by the previous owners' name—*the Taylor House*.

She spoke about how enjoyable it has been to live in this area, noting how much she especially loved listening to all the personal histories and memories shared during our Sunday gatherings.

She expressed her hope to contribute to that tradition—though few of us were ready for the tale she was about to unleash.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Her boyfriend, who was serving a full-time mission at the time, had sent her an audio cassette tape sharing updates about his daily life.

It started out innocently enough, with him recounting his routines as a missionary. But as the recording went on, he began dropping subtle hints—implying that the life of a non-missionary back home was somehow more relaxing, perhaps even a bit inferior to the selfless, dedicated work of a full-time minister.

The more she listened, the more her blood began to boil. By the time the tape reached the end, she was absolutely furious.

Determined not to let his comments slide, she decided to fire off an immediate response in the exact same medium. For sixty—or maybe ninety—uninterrupted minutes, she poured her absolute fury into that microphone.

When the session was finally over, feeling vindicated, she decided to rewind the tape to review the recording before popping it into an envelope.

She hit play.

*Silence.*

Surprisingly, the tape was completely blank. Not a single word had been recorded—whether by technical oversight or sheer divine intervention.

She took the blank tape as a sign from above.

Cooling off, she decided to scale back her response and write a much gentler reply instead.

Without that recording failure, she’d probably be married to a different fellow today—and she wouldn't be occupying the old Taylor home, or looking back on the memories of raising eight children alongside that very same missionary.

![](images/20250218_094906.jpg)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

> *“Not that which goeth into the mouth defileth a man; but that which cometh out of the mouth, this defileth a man.”* — Matthew 15:11

We need to exercise restraint and be circumspect as we compose our thoughts into writing.

However, as the Savior’s teaching suggests—and as our neighbor's blank cassette tape proved—it is one thing to draft an incendiary email or outline a provoking text in the heat of passion.

It is far more damaging to actually react and send that response without a proper review.

Back then, a technical glitch—or perhaps a bit of quiet divine intervention—saved a young woman from sending ninety minutes of unedited anger, preserving a marriage and a future family of ten in the process.

Today, our messages don't travel on slow mail, recorded on analog cassette tapes and placed in paper envelopes; they move instantly through the internet.

It makes one wonder: will future AI serve as our modern guardian angel, running a 12-point safety check for emotional intelligence or flagging an anger alert before launching our impulsive words into irretrievable orbit?

Will we need to return to drafting our messages in quiet, storing them in a folder labeled *To Be Reviewed*?

Perhaps the words to that hymn, *"His Eye Is on the Sparrow,"* hold a clue:

> Though by the path He leadeth, But one step I may see: His eye is on the sparrow, And I know He watches me;

Step by step, word by word, we will follow Him—for He is watching and walking with us.
